title: AI-assisted conflicts and independence clearance across a multi-firm accounting network
problem: A private-equity-backed accounting network must clear conflicts and independence across member firms, which rely on spreadsheets, manual processes and long completion times before an engagement letter goes out.
approach: Crete Professionals Alliance feeds member-firm data into one warehouse; Intapp Conflicts uses AI risk-scoring so compliance staff focus on high-risk results.
The compliance team reviews high-risk results and decides remediation; potential independence issues are escalated to partners.
No time, accuracy or error figure is published (vendor-published); executives say the approach will relieve staff.

title: Risk-scored acceptance and continuance workflow with automated data pull and AI summaries
problem: Acceptance and continuance decisions draw on independence, conflict, reputational and know-your-client information held in separate systems and often handled in Excel and email.
approach: Intapp and Kingland sell risk-scored questionnaires and reviewer routing; Intapp adds AI request summaries, Kingland does not say which steps use AI.
Risk teams review and approve when risk is detected, and decisions route to reviewers for sign-off.
No customer result, time saving or error rate is published (vendor-published); a 2024 academic prototype outputs a risk level as decision support.

title: AI-powered client lifecycle platform joining client checks and engagement acceptance
problem: Client onboarding, due diligence and engagement acceptance at a large audit and advisory firm sit in separate steps with manual hand-offs.
approach: Grant Thornton UK selected Fenergo's AI platform to join client checks, due diligence and acceptance; the AI's decisions are not described.
Vendor says it removes thousands of hours of manual effort (vendor-published); the firm says it will speed engagement starts (self-reported).
Who signs off the acceptance decision is not stated in either release.

title: AI-assisted anti-money-laundering onboarding: document sorting, risk scoring and sanctions hit triage
problem: Onboarding information arrives by unstructured email, often incomplete, and sanctions and politically-exposed-person screening produces false matches that staff clear by hand.
approach: A vendor prototype entering pilot uses AI document classification to feed a client risk-scoring model; a language-model pipeline filters false screening hits.
The vendor says the compliance officer receives cases already triaged; the money laundering reporting officer decides on suspicious activity reports.
No accuracy or time-saving figure is published (vendor-published); trial firms are unnamed and not described as audit firms.

title: AI extraction of client ownership structures into family trees for independence checks
problem: Independence and conflict checks depend on a complete map of a client's affiliates, often built by hand; IFIAR counted 11 findings in 2025 on unreliable tracking.
approach: Kingland says its tool uses AI to read client documents and extract ownership details into a family tree the user completes.
The tool walks professionals through building the tree, so a person confirms the structure.
Vendor says it gives a single source of truth for entity records; no measured result (vendor-published).

title: Independence monitoring dashboards, breach management and personal-holdings checks
problem: Independence is checked only at points in time, so emerging issues surface late; IFIAR recorded 22 findings in 2025 on failing to monitor staff and partner personal independence.
approach: Kingland describes dashboards joining independence, risk and engagement data plus a breach workflow; its only named AI function reads broker statements.
Independence, risk and service-line leaders act on the trends shown.
Vendor says new holdings are checked within 24 hours of a trade (vendor-published); broker-feed automation, not AI, with no measured result.

title: Partner rotation candidate matching that excludes people the independence rules bar
problem: Rotation planning must balance experience, availability and career stage against independence limits on who can take over a client.
approach: Kingland describes a tool that surfaces suitable candidates from experience, availability and career data, and excludes people the independence rules bar.
Firm leaders make the rotation decision; the tool provides a view of candidates.
Vendor says it gives a clear view of top candidates; no measured result (vendor-published).

title: Automated engagement-letter production
problem: Engagement letters are produced for every audit and must reflect the engagement's terms.
approach: Some firms use an automated solution for engagement letters; the survey does not say whether AI is used.
Intapp markets automated creation and collection of engagement letters inside its acceptance product, without naming customers.
26% of surveyed firms have an automated engagement-letter solution (independent); this is automation, not necessarily AI.
The human checkpoint is not stated in the source.

title: Pricing and targeting engagements from historical firm data inside acceptance
problem: Intapp's white paper says firms treat acceptance and independence checking as a cost centre and asks whether they know the true cost of each engagement.
approach: Use historical firm data in automated acceptance to set prices and terms, target high-value clients and steer partners with whitelists and blacklists.
Potential revenue impact estimates: 1.5-4% informed pricing, 1-3% strategic targeting, 0.05-1.5% identifying conflicts (vendor-published; not measured results).
The human checkpoint is not stated in the source.

title: Idea: assess a client's reliance on AI in financial reporting at acceptance
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients increasingly use AI in financial reporting, so the auditor may be unable to gather evidence and management may not understand its own outputs.
approach: An AICPA practice aid says a client's AI use may affect acceptance or continuance; heavier reliance may mean more information is needed.
The AICPA says auditors should address client AI reliance at the start and check the team has the skills needed.
A new human assessment step, not AI doing the task; the partner and firm risk function decide. No firm practice found.

title: Idea: engagement terms covering the firm's AI use and client-data consent
problem: Idea, not a deployment: firms use AI on client work, but it is unclear when the engagement letter or a consent must say so.
approach: The AICPA practice aid says the US audit-terms standard does not require naming AI tools, though laws, contracts or policy may.
AICPA ethics staff say firms should ask whether client consent is needed before client data goes into an AI tool.
The partner decides what the engagement letter says and whether consent has been obtained. No firm practice was found.

title: Idea: tell audit committees about the auditor's AI use and independence implications
problem: Idea, not a deployment: the SEC's chief accountant says audit committees are asking about the independence implications of auditors' AI use.
approach: A firm's account of its AI tools, vendors and alliances would become part of its communication with those charged with governance.
The engagement leader would communicate with the audit committee. No firm describes a standard communication on this topic.

title: Idea: review AI tool-vendor contracts and licences for independence before adopting them
problem: Idea, not a deployment: tool vendors can shift control, judgment, fees or evidence access away from the auditor, creating undue-influence and self-interest threats.
approach: Before adopting a vendor, review contracts for cross-referral concentration, vendor involvement in the work, payment for evidence access and marketing control.
A commentator proposes recording who owns each vendor, what the firm pays, and whether the vendor can train models on client data.
The independence partner concludes and documents the evaluation. No firm was found that has published such a review.

title: Idea: check firm-wide AI-vendor alliances against audit-client lists
problem: Idea, not a deployment: networks have firm-wide AI vendor alliances, and the SEC's chief accountant says it gets complicated when a firm's non-audit partner uses an audit client.
approach: Independence teams would map AI-vendor relationships against audit-client and affiliate lists before signing and at each acceptance or continuance.
Context: Deloitte is making Claude available to 470,000 people, KPMG to more than 276,000 staff (vendor-published); scale, not an outcome.
No firm process was found; the suggested check is global independence leadership sign-off and audit-committee dialogue.

title: Idea: permissibility gate for AI services offered to audit clients
problem: Idea, not a deployment: firms are expanding AI services to clients they may also audit, and building or hosting AI for an attest client can raise independence concerns.
approach: Route every proposed AI build, host, licence or assurance service through pre-approval, checking self-review threats, management responsibility and commercial dependency.
Deloitte Ireland and Luxembourg describe pre-approval workflows, but none is described as AI-specific; applying the gate to AI services is the idea.
Independence and conflicts teams review before approval, and the audit partner evaluates threats and safeguards.

title: Independence due diligence and governance safeguards before taking private-equity investment
problem: Private-equity investment enters the profession mainly through alternative practice structures, and IFAC says new governance layers can dilute audit partners' control over client selection.
approach: AICPA guidance describes due diligence before the deal, an expert-drafted administrative services agreement, independence monitoring and a multipronged independence evaluation.
Grant Thornton UK's Cinven investment closed in early 2025 after regulatory approval, with the audit practice kept in its LLP.
This is a human control process, not AI; the FRC asks firms to engage early and with full candour.
Context: 385 transactions in 2025, 139 involving audit firms (independent); a measure of structural change, not of the review step.
who: Grant Thornton UK, AICPA, IFAC, FRC

title: Screen clients against the investor group; consult the regulator on grey areas
problem: When a firm's owner or its funds hold stakes in companies, taking those or related companies as audit clients can fall into independence grey areas.
approach: At acceptance the firm checks links to the investor's holdings, declines where independence is doubtful and consults the regulator on unclear cases.
Grant Thornton UK's chief executive said the firm would not audit a company in which owner Cinven has invested (self-reported).
One reported case: the FRC agreed a prospective client was a grey area and the firm did not proceed (self-reported).
Independence and risk leaders assess whether the investor or its staff are covered persons; no source describes AI in this screening.

title: AI audit platform launched by Grant Thornton in an alternative practice structure
problem: In an alternative practice structure the non-attest entity can supply the attest firm with technology, so a shared AI platform raises who provides it and whether independence rules apply.
approach: Grant Thornton LLP announced gtap on 7 May 2026, a cloud audit platform with AI workflows and agents surfacing risks and anomalies.
It starts on private-company audits, expanding to public-company audits the next year; the firm says professionals supervise every step.
The CEO says automating transactional work lets teams focus on judgment; no measured result (self-reported).
Idea only: treat shared platforms as part of the independence assessment, with attest-firm leadership approval.

title: Investor-funded holding company building AI audit tooling and investing in audit firms
problem: Audit tools and workflows have not meaningfully changed in decades, according to Modus's CEO, and Lightspeed's partners say public accounting has been underserved by technology.
approach: Modus raised $85 million (vendor-published), led by Lightspeed, to invest in audit-first firms and build AI-enabled audit tooling.
It has invested in one top-200 firm and, according to Lightspeed, has deployed seven AI workflows there (vendor-published).
No audit-quality or efficiency result is reported; the human checkpoint is not stated in the source.

title: New audit firms built around AI from the start
problem: Auditing has been slower than other professions to absorb automation and still relies on manual collection, matching and documentation, according to coverage of Repodo's launch.
approach: Repodo, a Copenhagen audit firm, raised EUR 8.2 million pre-seed (vendor-published); AI systems are meant to handle much of the repetitive work.
Oath Verified raised about $10 million in total (vendor-published) and uses an alternative practice structure because its platform company is venture-backed.
Licensed professionals keep judgment, oversight, the signature and final responsibility; no client, quality or independence result is published.

title: Audit fee renegotiation justified by AI-enabled efficiency
problem: Audit has been priced on hours, seniority and review depth; if AI speeds execution, clients may expect lower fees.
approach: KPMG International reportedly negotiated a lower audit fee from Grant Thornton UK, arguing AI would cut costs (unnamed sources, Financial Times).
Fee 14% lower, from $416,000 to $357,000, per KPMG International's filing (independent); the link to AI rests on unnamed sources.
Commentators split between holding fees because humans validate and sign off, and moving to subscription or continuous audit-as-a-service pricing.
